This research introduces a novel Bayesian approach to a network autoregression model that accounts for the interconnected nature of data. By employing a hierarchical prior distribution, we can identify and model the underlying network structures within the data. Our proposed model is then applied to a real-world case study involving the daily interactions of a specific stock's investors and their impact on its value.

The overwhelming amount of scientific information available today presents a significant obstacle to verifying the accuracy of scientific statements. To address this issue, we have developed a new method for automatically verifying the validity of scientific claims. Our approach involves the use of a sophisticated neural network capable of processing both short and long text inputs. The network is pre-trained on a substantial dataset of 1.2 million verified scientific statements. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we have created a new test dataset consisting of 1,000 scientific claims. Our results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing models, achieving a 0.83 F1-score. Furthermore, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of our method's performance across various domains and tasks, including the evaluation of scientific negations.

A novel, deep learning-based method for segmenting the human eye's key structures using optical coherence tomography (OCT) images is introduced. This approach enables the precise identification of the macula, photoreceptors, inner retinal layers, and the optic nerve head in OCT scans. By utilizing a U-Net architecture and refining the output with a boundary detection technique, the method effectively segments the eye's structures. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through its application to two publicly available datasets, resulting in accurate segmentations that closely match those obtained from advanced imaging software.

This paper introduces a novel approach to cognitive modeling by incorporating a temporal element. It enables the simultaneous modeling of multiple tasks and their sequence of execution within a single model. The proposed framework, known as the Temporal Cognitive Model, is a versatile extension of existing models, such as the Cognitive Model, and can be seamlessly integrated with various loss functions and optimizers. The model's performance is demonstrated through its application to a range of tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, as well as the evaluation of tasks within a fixed sequence or varying order. The results show that the Temporal Cognitive Model outperforms its static counterparts, achieving state-of-the-art results in tasks with predefined sequences and improved performance in tasks with variable orderings. The model's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/andre-ruffaldi/temporal-cognitive-model.

This research delves into the properties of Mersenne primes through the lens of Mautner System theory. We establish a new theorem, dubbed the Eight Levels Theorem, which mirrors the Eightfold Way Theorem by S. Golomb. Furthermore, this work introduces the concept of Mersenne prime walks and demonstrates that Mersenne prime walks adhere to Mautner System theory. We also derive a novel theorem, specifically the Mersenne Prime Walks Theorem, which mirrors the Mersenne Prime Theorem.

This research paper explores the derivation of the first-order hydrodynamic equation from the 13-velocity Boltzmann equation. It is demonstrated that the 13-velocity model is capable of accurately capturing the behavior of gases at both low and high velocities, as well as in situations involving both rarefaction and high density. The derivation process involves solving a set of linear equations to obtain the first-order hydrodynamic conserved quantities. The resulting hydrodynamic equation is shown to be hyperbolic, with its eigenvalues and eigenvectors explicitly calculated. The validation of the 13-velocity model involves comparing its numerical solutions to those of the Navier-Stokes model and the 7-velocity model. The results of these comparisons indicate that the 13-velocity model outperforms the others, particularly in scenarios involving high velocity and high density.

We have conducted a study of the carbon lines in a sample of 15 galaxies at a redshift of 0.5-1.0 using the Keck Cosmic Web Imager. This is the first time that high-resolution spectroscopy has been used to measure the carbon lines in these galaxies. We have found that the carbon lines are not in a state of local thermodynamic equilibrium, which is a common assumption made in many studies. This assumption can lead to incorrect estimates of gas temperatures, with some temperatures being as high as 10,000 Kelvin. We have also found that the carbon lines are sensitive to the metallicity of the gas, which is a key factor in understanding the chemical evolution of the universe. This is particularly important for studying galaxies at high redshifts, where metallicity can be difficult to determine. We have used the carbon lines to estimate the metallicity of the gas in our sample galaxies and found that they are consistent with the metallicity measured from other spectral lines. This suggests that the carbon lines can be used as a reliable indicator of metallicity in galaxies at high redshifts.

This study presents a novel approach to active learning, specifically designed for the task of code-switching detection in low-resource languages. The method, known as CAL, employs a combination of two techniques: CAL-Confidence, which identifies the most uncertain samples for human annotation, and CAL-Adversary, which uses a discriminator to select challenging samples that are easily mistaken by the model. The proposed technique has been successfully applied to the ASAR dataset, which contains a mix of Arabic and English text, and has demonstrated the potential for improvement through active learning, with the model achieving a 1.5% reduction in error rate on average after each round.

Young solar-type stars are known to emit X-rays, which can impact the surrounding circumstellar discs. This research aims to investigate the effects of X-ray irradiation on the formation of dust structures in these discs. Using a 2D radiation-hydrodynamic model, we simulate the evolution of discs under varying X-ray conditions and analyze the resulting dust structures. Our findings indicate that X-ray irradiation can lead to the formation of dust structures, which are influenced by the disc's mass, the X-ray flux, and the disc's height. These structures are primarily formed through the creation of a pressure gradient driven by X-ray heating, which is more pronounced in discs with higher X-ray fluxes. Our results suggest that X-ray irradiation can lead to the formation of ring-like structures, which are consistent with observations of young stars.

This research introduces a family of high-order, explicit generalized-$\alpha$ methods for solving hyperbolic problems. The proposed methods are characterized by their ability to maintain stability at large time steps and achieve second-order accuracy in the absence of damping. This is in contrast to traditional generalized-$\alpha$ methods, which are first-order accurate. The new methods are derived from a modified generalized-$\alpha$ scheme and are shown to converge to a second-order method as the damping parameter approaches zero. The convergence is demonstrated using a theoretical analysis and verified through numerical experiments.

We investigate the behavior of a single impurity within a weakly interacting three-dimensional bosonic environment, using a combination of the self-consistent coupled equations and the multilayer multiconfigurational self-consistent Hamiltonian method. Our findings, based on these numerical approaches, are in line with the predictions of the Bose-Hubbard polaron model. We observe that as the coupling between the impurity and the environment increases, the polaron's mass grows, the effective mass increases, and the residual interaction becomes stronger. Our numerical results also show that the polaron's residue is inversely proportional to the square of the coupling strength, in agreement with the weak-coupling theory. We further find that the polaron's residue is directly proportional to the square of the boson density, consistent with the predictions of the Bose-Hubbard polaron model. Our study also reveals that the polaron's residue is inversely proportional to the square of the boson density, consistent with the predictions of the Bose-Hubbard polaron model.

This study develops a probabilistic model to analyze the distribution of relief supplies in response to Hurricane Maria's impact on Puerto Rico. The model incorporates data from the US Census Bureau, the Puerto Rico Planning Board, and the Puerto Rico Department of Health to estimate the population's access to relief items such as food, water, and shelter. The results indicate that the distribution of these supplies was highly unevenly allocated across different regions of Puerto Rico.

We have developed a new method for efficiently computing and optimizing the evaluation of gravitational wave signals from supermassive black hole binaries in pulsar timing array data analysis. This method involves the use of fast Fourier transforms and a specific approach to evaluating the log-determinant function, which is used in Bayesian inference for pulsar timing array data. We compared the performance of our new method to two existing methods and found that it produces results at least an order of magnitude faster, while achieving similar accuracy. This method has been implemented in the Evaneshence software package and is available for public use.

In Bayesian coordination games with a single deviation property, we examine how unique Bayesian-Nash equilibria are maintained when private information about action payoffs is incomplete. We find that if this private information is sufficiently accurate, the unique equilibrium remains unchanged. Conversely, if private information is too limited, the unique equilibrium may disappear. We demonstrate that if private information is too restricted, the unique equilibrium becomes a Bayesian-Nash equilibrium in a modified game where payoffs are redefined to incorporate public information. This outcome arises because the unique equilibrium is also a Nash equilibrium in this modified game. We further show that if private information is sufficiently accurate, the unique equilibrium is also a unique Nash equilibrium in the original game.

Terahertz spectroscopy has become a crucial tool in various fields, including medicine, security, and chemistry, but its applications are often hindered by the presence of water. Water's complex far-infrared properties make it difficult to model and separate from the desired signals. To address this challenge, we developed a new method that utilizes a deep neural network to identify and eliminate water's influence on terahertz spectroscopy data. Our approach involves training the network with simulated data and evaluating its performance on both synthetic and real-world measurements. The results demonstrate the network's ability to accurately remove water's contribution, allowing for the extraction of valuable information from the data.

The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the importance of developing emergency response tools that can be deployed immediately, without requiring extensive setup. To address this need, we introduce a novel AI-powered tool that enables rapid, real-time risk assessment. By harnessing the capabilities of a pre-trained BERT-Large model, we have successfully created a system that can accurately predict the likelihood of COVID-19 transmission based on social media posts. To validate the effectiveness of our tool, we conducted a comparative analysis with existing AI-powered systems, which demonstrated its superior performance in predicting infection risk. Furthermore, our tool has been successfully deployed in multiple countries, generating over 100 million predictions to date.

A novel, multi-resolution approach to particle hydrodynamics simulation has been developed to tackle complex interactions between dynamic structures and fluids. This innovative method leverages a unique combination of two distinct particle-based techniques: one that accurately models the intricate details of structures and fluids, and another that efficiently simulates their interactions on a larger scale. By seamlessly integrating these two approaches, the new method effectively captures the nuanced behavior of systems and optimizes computational efficiency. To validate its effectiveness, the researchers applied their technique to a variety of challenging scenarios, including interactions between multiple objects and fluids, and observed accurate results in all cases.

Topological insulators are characterized by unique properties, including the protection of their surface states and the presence of gapless Dirac points. These features enable the efficient transfer of information through low-resistance pathways. In this study, we examine the transport behavior of a specific type of topological insulator, known as the 3D 8-nanotube, and compare it to that of a non-topological insulator, the 3D 8-nanotube with a gapped Dirac point. The results show that the topological insulator exhibits superior performance, with significantly higher conductivity and a much lower thermal resistance. These findings suggest that topological insulators are ideal candidates for developing high-performance devices.

The HEP Software Foundation's Physics Event Generator Working Group has developed a report to inform the High-Luminosity LHC review process, focusing on long-term prospects for physics at the HL-LHC. The report highlights the benefits of a p+p reference collision system and recommends the adoption of a comprehensive software infrastructure to ensure the reliability of HL-LHC physics data. The report is available online in its final version.
We demonstrate the ergodicity of a certain subset of mean-value functions that satisfy specific conditions, building upon earlier work by Takagi (2008) which partially addressed this problem.

We have conducted a thorough investigation of the 166.5 MHz thermal OH emission in the outer Galaxy, utilizing the Green Bank Telescope. Our analysis of the 8$^{\circ}$ $\times$ 4$^{\circ}$ region of the outer Galaxy, situated at a distance of 3.5 kpc, has yielded several key findings. Firstly, we have identified a large-scale, diffuse structure of molecular gas spanning approximately 100 parsecs, characterized by a flat gas distribution. Our results also indicate that the OH emission is consistent with a model of a thin gas disk, with the gas height decreasing as the distance from the Galactic center increases. Furthermore, we have discovered a significant correlation between the OH emission and the CO emission in the outer Galaxy, suggesting a close relationship between the OH and CO emissions. Our data also reveal a complex structure of molecular gas, with the OH emission being more concentrated in the direction of the spiral arms.

This research examines a model of consumer preferences that are influenced by the distribution of wages in the economy, leading to a closed-form solution for optimal consumption and a wage distribution that is consistently derived. The model is then used to analyze the impact of a progressive tax system on the economy, considering the effects on the Pareto optimal tax rate and the resulting wage distribution. The model is also adapted to incorporate heterogeneous consumer preferences and a diverse set of goods, leading to a generalization of the optimal consumption and wage distribution. The model is then used to estimate the Pareto optimal tax rate and the resulting wage distribution in the United States, providing an explanation for the observed U-shaped tax curve.

We investigate the behavior of a two-dimensional system consisting of polar active particles that interact through a repulsive potential. By employing a hydrodynamic model and analyzing the system's dynamics, we identify the conditions under which it exhibits a transition from a disordered state to an ordered state characterized by a non-zero overall polarization. This transition is marked by a continuous change in polarization and occurs at a specific non-zero value of activity. Furthermore, we find that the system's behavior near the transition exhibits a specific pattern of fluctuations, characterized by a particular relationship between different types of correlations.

The decay process of the doubly charmed baryon, specifically its transformation into a charmed baryon, an electron, and a positron, is analyzed using a Lagrangian model that incorporates heavy baryon chiral perturbation theory and vector dominance. Calculations for the decay width, along with branching ratios, were performed and the results are presented. Notably, the decay width of the charmed baryon, specifically its transformation into a charmed baryon, an electron, and a positron, was determined to be $1.93\times10^{-16}$ GeV, with branching ratios of the charmed baryon, specifically its transformation into a charmed baryon, an electron, and a positron, when decaying from the doubly charmed baryon, found to be $0.11$, $0.11$, and $0.02$, respectively.

This paper examines a cooperative localization problem in which an observer seeks to determine their location by utilizing a locator's distance measurements. The locator's goal is to provide the observer with accurate distance readings, while the observer must interpret this information to identify their position. Both the locator and the observer are unaware of each other's knowledge and must rely on communication to achieve their goals. The localization process is modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process, and we propose a cooperative localization algorithm based on the principles of Bayesian inference and the Riemannian geometry of manifolds. The algorithm is evaluated through simulations in a 2-dimensional environment, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

A novel approach for analyzing rotating machinery is presented, which involves
extracting key features from time-domain signals and then using a ranking system
to identify the most relevant ones. This method, which is based on the band
relevance factor, pinpoints the most informative frequency bands within the
vibration signal. By employing a novel feature extraction technique, which is
based on the Hilbert-Huang Transform, the method is able to extract a wide range
of features that are then ranked and selected for further analysis. This
approach is then compared with other existing methods, which are found to be
less effective. The efficacy of the method is demonstrated through its
application to a real-world case study involving a pump, which is used to
demonstrate its ability to accurately diagnose problems.

A study of CaTSi3 (where T is either Pt or Ir) has been conducted using muon spectroscopy to examine the superconducting properties of these compounds.  The results indicate that these compounds maintain time-reversal symmetry, as the muon-spin relaxation data do not exhibit a gap.  The superfluid density of CaTSi3 was determined through muon spin rotation, and the findings suggest that these compounds possess a relatively weak superconducting coupling.  The superfluid density of CaPtSi3 was found to be lower than that of CaIrSi3, and the findings align with theoretical predictions that suggest a unique s-wave gap structure in these compounds.

This paper presents a novel approach to solving optimal control problems using sparse grids.  The proposed method employs a sparse grid to approximate the state and control functions, which significantly reduces the computational complexity compared to a dense grid.  Leveraging the sparse grid's superior properties, this method enables the efficient computation of optimal control solutions.  The proposed method is validated through numerical experiments on diverse optimal control problems, which demonstrate its efficacy and accuracy.

A novel approach to density estimation is presented, which employs a neural 
network with a hierarchical structure to model the density of data at different 
scales. This framework is rooted in the concept of free energy and utilizes 
a single loss function that can be optimized through a single training process. 
The method is versatile and can be applied to various neural network 
architectures, including those with complex hierarchical structures. The proposed 
approach is evaluated on diverse datasets, encompassing both synthetic and 
real-world data, and is found to yield superior results in terms of density 
estimation accuracy.

The shift to renewable energy in electric power systems is driven by climate change mitigation efforts, but it also introduces new challenges in modeling and controlling these systems. The current approaches are inadequate for handling the complexities of low-carbon systems, where traditional methods fall short. In this research, we develop a new framework for modeling and controlling hierarchical power systems, taking into account the interconnectedness of renewable energy sources and load management. Our approach is based on a multi-agent system that enables real-time information exchange and coordinated control, ensuring that the system operates within predetermined limits. The proposed method is tested in a simulation of the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) system, demonstrating its ability to adapt to changing conditions and its potential to reduce emissions.

We have developed a novel Monte Carlo algorithm for the two-dimensional percolation model, which enables efficient sampling of states with a fixed number of connections for sites and bonds separately. Our algorithm is capable of generating samples with a high degree of precision, as evidenced by its successful application to various statistical distributions. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have applied our algorithm to study the largest cluster in the system and the spatial correlations of connected sites and bonds. Our results show that the algorithm is a reliable tool for analyzing percolation models and can be used to validate theoretical predictions about the system's behavior.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is crucial for maintaining optimal conversion rates and extending reactor lifespan.  However, temperature fluctuations can arise due to uneven heat transfer, varying gas flow, and changes in the bed's moisture content.  To address this issue, researchers have developed a novel control strategy that utilizes a model-based approach to regulate temperature fluctuations in catalytic fixed bed reactors.  This control strategy relies on a predictive model, which forecasts temperature fluctuations within the bed, taking into account the impact of gas flow, heat transfer, and moisture content.  By utilizing this model, the control strategy can accurately identify the source of temperature fluctuations and apply targeted interventions to rectify the issue.  In a series of experiments, the control strategy successfully reduced temperature fluctuations by up to 50% and increased the overall conversion rate by up to 10% compared to conventional control methods.

We investigate the phenomenon of reentrant superconductivity in a two-dimensional model, specifically in the context of a system exhibiting both s-wave and d-wave superconducting properties. Our analysis focuses on the superconducting phase diagram in the presence of a magnetic field, with particular interest in the interplay between s-wave and d-wave superconductivity. Notably, the system exhibits reentrant superconductivity when subjected to a magnetic field, with the transition point influenced by the interplay between s-wave and d-wave superconductivity.

This research explores the application of deep Q-learning in ultra-wideband (UWB) wireless networks, focusing on the energy-efficient routing of data packets. The study addresses the challenge of minimizing energy consumption while maximizing the reception of data packets in UWB networks, with a dynamic and uncertain wireless channel. The proposed deep Q-learning approach is evaluated against traditional routing methods, revealing a significant improvement in the reception of data packets and a reduction in energy consumption.

We have developed a new approach to clustering that focuses on the shape of the data rather than just its location. This method, called shape clustering, involves grouping points under specific distance metrics, such as the Hausdorff or geodesic metric, and finding the optimal cluster centers. Our research specifically targeted the $k$-median problem under the Hausdorff distance, which we found to be computationally hard, and we developed a constant-factor approximation algorithm for solving it. Our approach relies on a novel dynamic programming technique that can handle dynamic data, and we also showed that the $k$-median problem under the geodesic distance is APX-hard. However, we found that the problem becomes more manageable when the underlying graph is either planar or has bounded treewidth, and we developed efficient algorithms to tackle these cases.

Reinforcement learning for multiple agents is a complex problem due to its non-markovian and non-symmetric nature. To address this challenge, we developed a new method called MARL-RLS, which uses a memory-based approach to enable multi-agent reinforcement learning. This method utilizes a memory mechanism to store and manage information from other agents, allowing it to achieve better results. We tested MARL-RLS in a scenario where two agents must work together to navigate a maze while avoiding collisions. The results show that MARL-RLS outperforms a baseline version that lacks the memory mechanism, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving performance.

We establish an exponential-time bound for satisfiability checking in the context of fixpoint logics with variable dependence, which encompasses the most commonly studied fixpoint logics including FI, FIQO, and FOL. This result has significant implications for the study of the complexity of constraint languages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the satisfiability problem for the fixpoint logic FOL can be reduced to a problem with a specific structure, known as a tree-structured satisfiability problem, in a manner that preserves the complexity of the problem. This reduction is instrumental in establishing an exponential-time bound for the satisfiability problem in FOL.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian approach to signal recovery that leverages the principles of nonparametric hierarchical models. The proposed method incorporates a sparse matrix factorization of the measurement matrix, achieved through a combination of sparse priors and hyperpriors. The resulting Bayesian framework is then adapted to tackle the generalized linear inverse problem, encompassing a diverse range of signal reconstruction tasks. The efficacy of the method is demonstrated using a range of examples, including image deblurring, photo de-masking, and hyperspectral unmixing.

Air pollution poses a significant global health concern, particularly in urban areas, and continuous monitoring is essential to mitigate its effects. However, traditional air quality monitoring systems are often expensive and impractical to deploy in large public spaces. To address this issue, a drive-by sensing approach has been proposed, which leverages the data collected from a moving vehicle equipped with air quality monitoring equipment to create a comprehensive map of urban air quality. This study presents a new algorithm for constructing such a map, which takes into account the complex interactions between air pollution sources and the flow of pollutants in the environment. By modeling these dynamics as a complex network, the algorithm can accurately estimate the air quality across the urban area. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, a large-scale dataset was collected in Paris, France, and the resulting air quality map was compared to the output of a widely used simulation model. The results show that the proposed algorithm can provide a highly accurate estimate of urban air quality, with a level of detail that traditional methods cannot match.

This paper explores the Weil representation of the generalized special linear group $G_{l,n}$, based on $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, to investigate the unitary irreducible highest weight modules of the affine Lie algebra $sl_{l+1}^{(2)}$. The Weil representation of $G_{l,n}$ is obtained through a specific twisted group action on the Weil representation of the metaplectic covering of $G_{l,n}$.

Persuasive content creation is a crucial aspect of advertising, and the ability to generate such videos with the aid of AI is a significant breakthrough. This research introduces a novel, three-step approach to creating AI-powered persuasive videos, involving the prediction of audience engagement, selection of engaging content, and optimization of that content for maximum impact. The first step utilizes a pre-trained model to forecast the viewers' emotional response to various video segments. Next, an algorithm identifies the most captivating elements that capture the viewers' attention while maintaining a neutral overall tone. Finally, a reinforcement learning-based model refines the selection by rearranging the video segments to maximize the predicted audience engagement. The proposed method was tested on a dataset of 1,500 YouTube videos, and the results demonstrate its superiority over current methods in predicting audience engagement.

We have developed a novel approach to simulate the behavior of trapped ions by combining the time-dependent variational principle with deep learning techniques. This method, known as the deep learning variational principle, enables us to accurately model the evolution of ions in a two-dimensional space, encompassing both internal and external influences. Our approach leverages a neural network to efficiently propagate a set of parameters that describe the ions' states, thereby minimizing the need for extensive numerical calculations. This method has been successfully applied to a system of two ions, with or without an external driving force, and has yielded results that closely match those obtained through traditional numerical simulations.

The rapid advancement of high-performance computing technology has significantly accelerated the capacity to simulate intricate biological systems, thereby enabling researchers to thoroughly investigate the relationships between system parameters and emergent behaviors. This capability is particularly valuable in computational neuroscience, where researchers utilize computational models to replicate neural networks and examine the effects of various parameters on network dynamics. This study presents a comprehensive review of high-performance computing tools and techniques employed in computational neuroscience, encompassing both open-source and commercial software platforms. The review delves into the underlying algorithms, presents case studies of neural network simulations, and examines the current state of high-performance computing infrastructure. Furthermore, it highlights the potential of high-performance computing to facilitate breakthroughs in neuroscience and outlines the challenges that must be addressed to optimize its impact.

This paper presents a comprehensive dataset called CAMO++ that expands on the original CAMO dataset to cater to the diverse needs of the camouflaged instance segmentation research community. Building upon the strengths of the previous dataset, CAMO++, offers a more extensive collection of high-quality images and annotations, encompassing a broader range of challenging scenarios. These enhancements include a substantial increase in the number of images, the incorporation of new attributes and labels, and the addition of more complex cases. To validate the effectiveness of CAMO++, we have conducted thorough experiments and achieved promising results. These findings demonstrate the potential of CAMO++ to drive further advancements in the field of camouflaged instance segmentation.

This research examines how certain modifications to the standard theory of superconductivity affect the London penetration depth. We've found that a certain type of violation of the Lorentz principle leads to a penetration depth that depends non-linearly on frequency and temperature.

Despite the growing interest in AI model explainability, there is a lack of research on how to effectively communicate failures in AI recommendations to end-users. In our study, we examine how to provide clear and actionable information about AI model failures to end-users, and identify that end-user descriptions of their expectations are particularly useful for pinpointing systematic failures in AI recommendations. We introduce a novel framework for collecting and analyzing end-user descriptions to better understand AI model failures, and test its effectiveness in a user study involving 32 participants. The results of our study indicate that end-user descriptions can be a valuable tool for pinpointing systematic failures in AI recommendations, and provide valuable insights for improving AI model explainability.

In object detection, the decision process is a crucial aspect that determines the reliability of the model's predictions. Although classification heads are designed to assess confidence, they can be misled by incorrect object hypotheses. To address this issue, we introduce a new decision head that evaluates the likelihood of a prediction being an actual object. This decision head is trained to maximize the probability of correct object predictions while minimizing false alarms. To achieve this, we utilize a novel loss function that combines the classification loss with a decision loss. This decision loss is based on the ratio of false alarms to correct object detections, which is calculated by re-scanning the image using the classification head. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed decision head significantly enhances the robustness of object detection models, particularly in challenging scenarios.

Deep neural networks are highly susceptible to subtle, adversarial manipulations that can deceive even the most advanced models. To counter this vulnerability, researchers have developed a range of adversarial training methods, but these approaches often come with a significant drawback: catastrophic overfitting, which occurs when a model becomes overly specialized in recognizing a limited number of adversarial patterns. To address this issue, we introduce a novel adversarial training technique that leverages the inherent diversity of adversarial examples to prevent overfitting. By employing a dual-stage training strategy that involves generating diverse adversarial patterns from a diverse set of input images, we can effectively mitigate the risk of overfitting and improve the robustness of our models. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing adversarial training methods, which often rely on a single reference image.

This research delves into the properties of Thakurta black holes, which form from the collision of two spinning black holes, and explores the possibility of creating such events in the universe. We found that Thakurta black holes can be formed when two spinning black holes merge, and their existence is possible in various mass ranges. We also discovered that Thakurta black holes can potentially form in the universe, and their existence may be linked to the merger of binary black holes. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that Thakurta black holes can eventually transform into ordinary black holes, and we calculated the timescale for this process.

We examine the long-term behavior of optimization algorithms that switch objectives frequently, operating within a continuous framework. By establishing criteria for convergence and the rate at which it occurs, we provide a comprehensive understanding. Furthermore, we develop a modified version of the subgradient method that can adaptively adjust its learning rate in real-time, ensuring convergence regardless of the frequency of objective changes. The proposed method is demonstrated to converge under a commonly accepted condition, even in the presence of random and frequent objective switches.

A key advantage of homomorphic encryption is its ability to perform computations on encrypted data without the need for prior decryption. However, this approach is hindered by the requirement for a trusted setup phase, which can be vulnerable to attacks if compromised. To address this limitation, researchers have explored the concept of bootstrapping, which enables independent ciphertexts to be combined into a single encrypted value that can be processed without decryption. Despite its potential, implementing secure bootstrapping is a complex task due to the need for a trusted setup phase and the development of efficient algorithms that minimize the number of required operations. In this study, we present a novel approach to secure bootstrapping using a single trusted setup phase and a more efficient algorithm that reduces the number of operations required. Our approach is based on a modified version of the Brakerski-Naehrig (BN) curve, which we have adapted to achieve secure bootstrapping with a single trusted setup phase. We have also developed a more efficient algorithm that minimizes the number of operations required, making it a promising solution for secure bootstrapping.

We investigate a rotationally symmetric random matrix ensemble with a confining potential given by $V(\rho) = \int_{0^\pm} \frac{1}{\rho\ln|\rho|}d\rho$, where the function $V(\rho)$ is defined by an integral that includes a small modification near zero and an upper cutoff. This potential generalizes the harmonic oscillator potential and leads to a specific, singular behavior in the eigenvalue density. We derive the joint eigenvalue distribution for this ensemble and show that it can be expressed as a product of two functions, $P_N(\lambda)$ and $Q_N(\lambda)$, which are determined by a set of recurrence relations. In the thermodynamic limit, the resulting density has a specific, singular form, with a density function that is proportional to $\ln|\lambda|^{-1/2}$.

High-dimensional quantum systems have the potential to facilitate quantum communication and computation, but they are difficult to study due to the limited tools available. We have developed a new method for generating high-dimensional quantum correlations in a system of two qutrits, which can be manipulated using optical components. Our approach allows us to create various high-dimensional entangled and non-entangled states, including some that cannot be produced using existing methods, and can be used to demonstrate high-dimensional quantum correlations. This research provides a practical framework for generating high-dimensional quantum resources and can be applied to various quantum communication and computation tasks.

Bell's theorem is often seen as a direct outcome of local causality, which itself is frequently equated with factorizability. However, we propose a modified understanding of local causality that remains compatible with factorizability, thereby allowing for a more nuanced examination of the relationship between local causality and Bell's theorem.

This study introduces a novel method for generating continuous-time videos, 
enabling the creation of smooth transitions between frames without being confined 
to predefined time intervals. Our approach builds upon the VideoGAN architecture, 
yet diverges in its application of discrete convolutional layers. We replace these 
layers with continuous filters, the temporal derivatives of which are used to 
calculate the next frame's image. Consequently, our model can produce frames 
at arbitrary time points, thus producing more realistic video sequences. The 
resulting video generator is a continuous-time system, capable of producing 
smooth transitions between frames. We validate the efficacy of our model by 
comparing it to the original VideoGAN and other state-of-the-art methods on 
the UCF101 dataset.

We establish a geometric characterization of the $\Theta$-correspondence in a finite reductive dual pair, specifically for pairs consisting of a general group and its symplectic or odd orthogonal counterpart. This characterization is achieved through the application of the orbit method, which enables us to determine the $\Theta$-correspondence by analyzing orbits of the dual pair within their respective projective spaces.

The 8th International Conference on Luminescence of Inorganic Solids (ILS 2022) took place in Beijing, China from October 9-14, 2022. The event brought together researchers from multiple fields, including materials science, biophysics, and medical physics, who explored the applications of thermoluminescence dosimetry in various settings, including space, medicine, and daily life. The conference highlighted the potential of using personal dosimeters to measure exposure to ionizing radiation in everyday environments and the challenges associated with accurately quantifying low-level doses. The participants also discussed the advancements in luminescence-based dosimetry for medical applications and the development of novel dosimetry techniques using specialized materials.
This paper examines a particular category of double phase problems on Heisenberg group, specifically those with singular coefficients.

A novel, compact, and low-cost ultrasound tomography system has been developed for non-invasive tumor imaging. The system consists of a water-filled tank surrounded by 64 ultrasound transmitters and 64 digital channels for signal reception. By transmitting and receiving multiple signals, the system can reconstruct 2D cross-sectional images using a filtered back-projection algorithm. The feasibility of this technology was demonstrated by successfully imaging a Styrofoam tumor with ultrasound, resulting in high image quality with notable features. The system's performance was evaluated using the contrast to noise ratio (CNR) and showed promising results, with a CNR of 20.8 dB achieved in the experiments. The system's capabilities were further explored by imaging various phantoms, including a Styrofoam tumor, a chicken liver, and a chicken breast, resulting in high-quality images with excellent contrast. The system's performance was evaluated using the CNR and showed a maximum value of 30 dB. The system's capabilities were further explored by imaging tumors with varying sizes and shapes, resulting in high-quality images with excellent contrast. The system's performance was evaluated using the CNR and showed a maximum value of 40 dB achieved in the experiments.

The widespread adoption of machine learning (ML) models has led to a growing interest in post hoc explanation techniques, despite their limitations. These methods often struggle with reliability and consistency, and their results can be misleading. To address these issues, we developed a novel approach called ML-ML, which involves training ML models to provide reliable explanations for other pre-trained models. By using this method, we can create ML-ML models with high accuracy and robustness, and they can be used to explain new data with high accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ML-ML models in terms of accuracy, robustness, and calibration, and they outperform existing methods in terms of robustness, particularly in the presence of adversarial explanations.

This paper delves into the concept of explanations for machine learning models, specifically focusing on the limitations of current methods used with neural networks. The existing approaches are often based on the model itself, which can be a major drawback. To address this, we introduce a novel method called Model-Agnostic Explanation, which relies solely on the input data and its corresponding output. Our approach is based on the idea that explanations can be represented as a weighted combination of the input data, which we call the ExExplanation. The ExExplanation can be obtained through a linear regression process, which we demonstrate to be effective in various scenarios. The performance of our method is evaluated on a range of datasets, including both synthetic and real-world data, and is shown to be robust and efficient.

In the study of TbInO$_3$, researchers have found that its ground state is composed of a nonmagnetic doublet, which is unusual for a compound with a large Tb$^{3+}$ magnetic moment. This discovery is significant because it contradicts the typical expectation that such compounds would be ferromagnetic at low temperatures. Instead, they exhibit characteristics of a quantum spin liquid state, which is often seen in compounds with smaller magnetic moments. The researchers have proposed that the nonmagnetic ground state is due to the strong interaction between the 4f and 5d electrons in TbInO$_3$, which is a feature of rare-earth perovskites.

We demonstrate that for surfaces with an interior in $\mathbb{R}^3$ moving according to the power-of-mean curvature formula, where the power is greater than $1/2$, a convex ancient solution exists. This convex ancient solution serves as a model for the long-term behavior of solutions to the power-of-mean curvature formula, provided the initial surface has sufficiently small curvature.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a crucial component in various computer vision applications. However, the traditional CNN architecture is limited by its sequential processing order, which can lead to a substantial increase in computational costs. To address this limitation, this study proposes a novel approach that enables the efficient implementation of convolutional layers on reconfigurable hardware platforms. By converting convolutional layers into the frequency domain and utilizing the element-wise multiplication operation, the proposed method significantly reduces the computational complexity of convolutional layers. To further optimize the processing efficiency, this study introduces a novel reconfigurable hardware design that leverages the inherent parallelism of the element-wise multiplication operation. As a result, the proposed hardware design achieves a substantial reduction in computational complexity, which is demonstrated through the implementation of a custom hardware accelerator. The proposed hardware accelerator is evaluated using a range of CNN models, which demonstrate the proposed design's ability to achieve a substantial reduction in computational complexity, while also providing a high degree of flexibility and scalability.

Deep clustering techniques have achieved remarkable success in extracting latent representations by integrating the strengths of multiple layers. However, current methods often overlook the relationships between layers, leading to suboptimal performance. This study introduces a novel deep clustering approach that incorporates a self-attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the contributions of different layers, thereby enhancing the quality of the extracted representations. The proposed method is evaluated on multiple datasets and outperforms state-of-the-art deep clustering techniques in terms of both quantitative and qualitative metrics.

Identifying potential risks is a critical component of risk management, and organizations must develop a robust process to effectively identify risks. This process should incorporate key elements, including risk assessment, analysis, and prioritization. It is also essential to have a clear understanding of the types of risks that may arise, and to have a defined scope for risk identification efforts. This process should be tailored to specific business areas and incorporate input from various stakeholders. The goal of risk identification is to pinpoint potential risks, assess their likelihood and potential impact, and prioritize them for management and mitigation efforts.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA) is an emerging field that uses geometric and topological tools to analyze complex datasets. It has shown great promise in identifying patterns in datasets and classifying their topological features. In this study, we investigate the potential of TDA to classify datasets from various scientific disciplines. We examine the effectiveness of persistent homology in distinguishing between different types of data and compare it with other machine learning methods. Our results suggest that TDA methods outperform traditional machine learning algorithms, particularly when dealing with complex datasets.

We investigate the concept of contrasimilarity, a fundamental yet understudied aspect of process theory. Contrasimilarity is a more comprehensive version of language equivalence, accounting for both observable and hidden behaviors of concurrent processes. In this study, we examine contrasimilarity within the context of the basic parallel process calculus, a widely accepted framework for modeling concurrent systems. Our analysis focuses on contrasimilarity as a bisimulation-like concept and explores its inherent properties. We also develop a comprehensive, algebraic framework for understanding basic parallel process calculus, encompassing both the original theory and an enhanced, more robust version with additional features.
We establish a representation of the string 2-group within the frame bundle of a string manifold, which enables the construction of a twisted string structure on any string manifold.

The ion-acoustic wave modulational instability and rogue wave characteristics are investigated in a two-component plasma system consisting of non-extensive electrons, thermal positrons, and warm ions. The non-extensive electrons are modeled by a model based on Tsallis statistics, while the warm ions are represented by a Maxwellian distribution. Using the reductive perturbation method, a nonlinear Schrödinger equation is derived, and its modulational stability is examined numerically. The influence of plasma parameters on fundamental ion-acoustic wave properties is also explored through numerical analysis.

The study of plasmas relies heavily on Alfv\'en waves, which are a fundamental aspect of magnetohydrodynamics. These waves have been extensively researched in both laboratory and space-based settings, with a focus on their linear properties. This paper presents a new approach to measuring the dispersion relation of Alfv\'en waves in a laboratory setting, utilizing a novel technique that combines a Faraday cup with a planar Langmuir probe. The results of this experiment are compared to previous studies and theoretical models, including those from the MHD and kinetic theories.

We investigate how ambipolar diffusion impacts the formation of gravoturbulent instability in a filamentary molecular cloud. We use a simplified model that accounts for ambipolar diffusion by linking the magnetic field and density through a constant factor. We then apply this model to a previously established simulation of gravoturbulent instability in a cloud and analyze how ambipolar diffusion affects the cloud's properties. Our findings show that ambipolar diffusion significantly accelerates the growth of gravoturbulent instability, leading to the formation of more compact and denser regions. We also find that ambipolar diffusion increases the amplitude of turbulent fluctuations and the rate of collapse in these regions.

The phenomenon where repeated projective measurements accelerate a quantum system's evolution is known as quantum Zeno effect. This paper explores the effect of continuous measurements on a two-level system undergoing decoherence. The impact of continuous measurement on the system's decoherence rate is investigated. The results show that continuous measurement can significantly speed up the system's decoherence. This effect is attributed to the influence of measurement outcomes on the system's evolution. The study also examines how continuous measurement affects the system's relaxation and revival dynamics. The findings reveal that continuous measurement can control the system's revival time. This research has implications for the control of quantum systems through measurement.

The coherence of a quantum system's states is a vital characteristic that can be measured in various experiments. In this research, we investigate the coherence of a specific type of quantum state, known as the W state, which is composed of multiple particles. We examine how the coherence of this state is affected by different types of interaction and measurement methods. Our findings indicate that the coherence of the W state is highly dependent on certain parameters and can be maximized under specific conditions. Furthermore, we discovered that the coherence of the W state is significantly affected by the direction of measurement and can be destroyed if the measurement basis is aligned with the system's interactions. Our results also show that the coherence of the W state can be preserved even when interacting with an environment, provided that the interaction is not too strong.

This research introduces a novel, decentralized algorithm for planning trajectories in multi-robot systems. The algorithm, called CARL (Collision-Avoiding Reciprocal Linear), enables linear system agents to create collision-free paths by establishing a safety zone between agents. In contrast to traditional methods, CARL achieves efficient computation and effective collision avoidance without relying on complex nonlinear systems. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations involving various planning scenarios.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation has been extensively researched in the field of autonomous driving, particularly in lane detection, but its practical application remains challenging due to domain discrepancies. This is because current methods fail to adequately address the intricate structure of lane detection, leading to subpar performance in cross-domain scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel approach called Cycle of Lane Detection (CoLD), which involves a two-stage process. Initially, we employ a pre-trained model to extract features from both source and target domains. Subsequently, we utilize a refined target model to generate pseudo labels for the target domain. This process is then iteratively refined through a cycle of feature learning and pseudo label refinement. This iterative refinement process enables the target model to adapt to the source domain's feature space. Experimental results on the BDD100k and Baidu datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in lane detection.

The process of a water drop falling onto a hydrogel surface, where particles are adhering to its surface, is studied. The findings indicate that the presence of these particles on the hydrogel surface significantly shortens the time it takes for the water drop to absorb, with their concentration affecting both the initial penetration and complete absorption times of the water. The results also show that the hydrogel's swelling rate can be accelerated by the presence of these particles.

This study delves into the connection between student collaboration and academic achievement in massive online courses, employing a dataset comprising over 1.1 million students from 15 MOOCs. By utilizing a novel approach combining machine learning and statistical models, we investigate the impact of various factors on this relationship, including course subject, student background, and social attributes. The results indicate that while collaboration is generally linked to improved academic outcomes, this association is contingent upon the specific course context and the student's level of engagement.

Radar Wind Profilers are widely used to study atmospheric dynamics due to their ability to measure high-altitude winds. However, their application is limited by the need for precise calibration. This research proposes a new method for calibrating these devices using a technique called the Pyhely method, which requires minimal data collection. The proposed approach involves a simplified data analysis process and can be applied to any Radar Wind Profiler. This research also presents a case study of a specific device in Bratislava, Slovakia, and compares its results to data from a nearby station.

The cluster, situated at a distance of 9.5 kiloparsecs, is characterized by a distinct group of stars with similar properties, including a specific spectral type and age. In the context of bilingual text mining, we examine the task of translating a given source sentence in one of our target languages using synthetic translations. These artificial translations are generated by manipulating existing, often imperfect reference translations. By leveraging these generated samples, we can improve the quality of our mined translations. We propose a novel approach that utilizes a large, multilingual language model to create high-quality synthetic translations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in enhancing the quality of mined translations, as evidenced by significant improvements in both automatic and human evaluations.

We investigate the evolution of entanglement in a complex system consisting of
a large number of qubits, where the system's behavior is influenced by both random
unitary fluctuations and dissipation due to interactions with an environment.
The competition between unitary and dissipative dynamics leads to distinct phases,
where the scaling of entanglement varies depending on the system's parameters.
We find that the entanglement in certain phases can grow exponentially with system
size, while in other phases it can remain localized, even in the thermodynamic limit.
Our results demonstrate that the presence of dissipation can enhance entanglement
and highlight the importance of dissipative dynamics in stabilizing many-body
entanglement.

In transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers, the interlayer hybridization is a crucial factor that can be controlled by external influences. We have developed a theoretical framework to study how this hybridization changes in response to electric fields. Our research reveals that when an electric field is applied perpendicularly, the hybridization increases significantly, resulting in the formation of a new energy band. This new band exhibits a unique chiral property, with its energy varying in a parabolic pattern, and its dispersion related to the electric field's strength. Furthermore, the application of an in-plane electric field has a minimal impact on the hybridization. Our findings suggest that these TMD heterobilayers possess the potential to be used in the creation of electrically tunable topological materials and spintronic devices.

This research explores the echo state property of quantum reservoir computing within a broader framework of open quantum systems. By utilizing the concept of a quantum Markov chain, we establish a comprehensive understanding of the echo state property in quantum reservoir computing. Our findings reveal that it is feasible to create a quantum reservoir that exhibits the echo state property under a variety of conditions, including when the initial state of the system is defined, when the system's initial state is unknown, and when the system's initial state is not specified. Our research also identifies a key criterion for determining the echo state property in quantum reservoir computing, which is based on the existence of a specific type of quantum Markov chain. Our findings provide a theoretical foundation for understanding the echo state property in quantum reservoir computing, which can be applied to a wide range of systems.

A novel integrated circuit has been developed, combining photonic waveguides and trapped single atoms within a high-quality vacuum chamber.  The device's design enables the efficient transfer of photons into a freely accessible atomic mode, allowing for the creation of stable atomic populations and long-lasting quantum entanglement between atoms.  The circuit's robustness was demonstrated through the successful implementation of quantum non-demolition measurements on atomic spin states, as well as the efficient transfer of light from atoms to waveguides.  The circuit's capabilities were further showcased through the successful implementation of a quantum teleportation protocol, which successfully transferred a qubit from an atom to a photonic wavepacket.  The circuit's design also allows for the integration of multiple atoms and the creation of complex quantum gates, making it an ideal platform for the development of quantum information processing systems.

This study presents a new approach to solving the Laplace equation on a rectangular domain, using a combination of the finite element method and a conjugate gradient algorithm. The proposed method is highly scalable and efficient, as it can fully leverage the strengths of both the finite element and conjugate gradient frameworks. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed method's performance is essentially unaffected by the size of the problem, and that it can be easily parallelized. To further improve efficiency, the authors also develop a new preconditioner that significantly reduces computational time. Experimental results on large, complex systems confirm the proposed method's superior performance compared to traditional solvers.

We investigate the stability of interacting dark energy models with a scalar field, and find that the critical point representing the current universe phase is inherently unstable due to the interaction term. This instability can be attributed to the higher effective exponent of the potential, $\eta$, which is positive in this case. We demonstrate that the interaction term can be eliminated by a specific field redefinition, and in this scenario, the stability properties are solely determined by the potential exponent, $\eta$. Furthermore, we show that the instability of the current era is a universal feature of interacting dark energy models, and occurs regardless of the specific interaction term.

We have identified a transient X-ray source in the galaxy NGC 7392, which is likely the result of a tidal disruption event. Our analysis of the data collected by the Swift-BAT and the Fermi Large Area Telescope indicates that the source exhibited a unique pattern of variability, which is characteristic of an outflowing TDE. Our findings suggest that the source is experiencing a complex interplay between an outflow and an accretion disk, which is causing the source to emit radiation at high energies. Our data also reveal a significant increase in the source's gamma-ray output, which is consistent with the idea that the outflow is driving the source's variability. Our analysis of the source's gamma-ray spectrum indicates that the outflow is producing a significant amount of energy, which is consistent with the idea that the outflow is driving the source's variability. Our findings provide strong evidence for the presence of an outflowing TDE and highlight the importance of multi-wavelength observations in understanding these events.

This research focuses on the behavior of acoustic waves in the presence of tiny gas bubbles, specifically in the early stages of their interaction. We have developed a mathematical framework to describe the bubble's motion, taking into account the changes in pressure caused by the bubble, and have found that this approach leads to a non-linear equation. We have investigated the properties of this equation and shown that its solutions can be represented as a combination of two distinct components. We have also examined the behavior of these solutions in the context of a specific initial condition, and have identified a key factor that determines the outcome.

The connection between stress and emotions is a complex one, influenced by various factors including the nature of the stressor, the individual's personality, and their coping mechanisms. To develop a more effective stress detection system, it's essential to consider these factors and how they impact emotion regulation. We propose a novel approach to stress detection that incorporates a stress-aware emotion model, leveraging the relationships between emotions and stress to improve performance. This method involves identifying key emotion features and using them to predict stress levels. We tested our approach on the REAT-DB dataset, which contains recordings of individuals discussing stress-related topics. Our results show that this approach outperforms traditional methods, achieving a 0.83 macro F1-score.

This paper introduces PanGEA, a versatile toolkit designed to facilitate the annotation of spatial navigation tasks. By utilizing PanGEA, users can create a wide array of navigation tasks, including text-based, visual, and text+visual combinations. The toolkit features a user-friendly interface that allows for efficient task creation, as well as a built-in server for processing and managing annotated data. PanGEA's annotation framework is highly adaptable, permitting its application across various domains, such as news articles, social media platforms, and online forums. Furthermore, the toolkit's annotation capabilities can be seamlessly integrated with existing visual grounding models, thereby enhancing their performance and reducing the need for manual data annotation. PanGEA is an open-source tool, available for public download at https://github.com/THU-KEGG/panGEA.

We have developed a new method to determine the star formation timescales of massive elliptical galaxies based on the number of type Ia supernovae they contain. This approach uses a mathematical model that simulates the growth of dark matter halos and the merging of galaxies, followed by the collapse of gas into these merged galaxies. The model then calculates the number of supernovae produced by each galaxy, based on the amount of gas available for star formation. The model's results match observations of the number of type Ia supernovae in galaxies, and the star formation timescales calculated from these results are consistent with those estimated from other methods, such as measuring the number of stars in galaxies. This suggests that the number of type Ia supernovae in galaxies can be used to determine their star formation timescales, and that this method can be used to determine the star formation timescales of massive elliptical galaxies.

This paper introduces a novel image reconstruction algorithm for compressive sensing, leveraging the benefits of non-convex regularization in sparse representation to enhance performance. By incorporating a sparsity-inducing $\ell_0$ norm as a penalty term, the proposed algorithm effectively mitigates the limitations of under-smoothness associated with $\ell_1$ norm-based approaches. Building on the foundation of the sparse representation classification (SRC) technique, the algorithm is refined through the incorporation of a penalty term and an iterative optimization process. Experimental evaluations conducted on both artificial and real-world images demonstrate the algorithm's superiority over existing $\ell_1$-norm based methods, with notable improvements in terms of both peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and edge preservation.

A novel approach to detecting facial skin lesions has been developed, which employs a two-stage semantic segmentation technique. The initial stage utilizes a pre-trained U-Net model to identify the location of skin lesions, while the subsequent stage leverages a ResNet-50 model to classify lesions as either benign or malignant. The proposed method incorporates a multi-modal framework that integrates contextual information from various color channels, enhancing the accuracy of lesion detection. The approach was tested on a dataset comprising images of 300 patients, which yielded an impressive 97.4% accuracy in lesion detection and a 0.88 score under the Area Under the Curve (AUC).

This research introduces a new family of codes known as PAC, which combines the advantages of polar and convolutional codes. The new codes, proposed in 2021, have shown promising results in terms of error correction, but their decoding complexity has been a major concern. To address this issue, we have developed an efficient decoding method for PAC codes that significantly reduces complexity. The proposed semi-parallel decoding algorithm achieves a substantial reduction in complexity, with a time complexity of $O(N \log N)$, which is comparable to that of convolutional codes. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using various metrics, including the bit error rate (BER) and frame error rate (FER), and our results show that PAC codes with this new decoding method outperform 5G polar codes and conventional convolutional codes in terms of error correction, while maintaining similar decoding efficiency.

Sequential recommenders have become increasingly popular for providing personalized recommendations by learning user preferences from sequential patterns in their historical interactions. However, a significant limitation of these models is their inability to effectively handle users with limited interaction histories, a problem known as the cold-start issue. To address this, we propose a new approach that utilizes a knowledge graph to provide additional information about users, items, and their relationships. This approach involves a two-stage learning process that first identifies relevant items based on user preferences and knowledge graph similarity, and then refines this process to improve predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on real-world datasets, showing that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

This paper examines the effects of ultra high energy cosmic rays on dark matter and cosmology, with a focus on theoretical and experimental advancements in the field. It covers recent developments in the energy spectrum, with an emphasis on the composition and arrival patterns of these cosmic rays. It also discusses the implications of these findings for the mass of dark matter and potential signatures in the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, the paper explores the connections between ultra high energy cosmic rays, the cosmic microwave background, and the acceleration of these cosmic rays.

The study of craters formed by impacting celestial bodies has been a long-standing area of research, but the effects of a projectile's shape on the resulting crater morphology have not been extensively explored. To address this knowledge gap, researchers have conducted a series of experiments using projectiles with different shapes, including spheres, ellipsoids, and irregular bodies. The experiments involved impacting a layer of sand with varying energy inputs, and the resulting crater morphologies were analyzed using X-ray Computed Tomography. The study found that the shape of the projectile has a significant impact on the crater's shape, size, and volume, with spherical projectiles producing the largest craters and irregular bodies producing the smallest. The experiments also revealed that the crater's shape is sensitive to the angle of impact, with head-on collisions producing the largest craters. The study's findings have implications for understanding the evolution of planetary systems and the formation of small celestial bodies in our solar system.

The task of identifying individuals through facial recognition in vehicle windshields poses significant challenges, particularly due to factors such as motion, varying lighting conditions, and obstructions. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a deep learning model to analyze and interpret the output of a single, highly accurate facial recognition system. This approach involves a two-stage process: first, the model detects and isolates the most relevant facial regions, and then it generates a confidence score to quantify its level of certainty. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by conducting a comprehensive evaluation on a large, real-world dataset, and our results indicate a notable improvement in accuracy, with a 10% increase in correct identifications and a 30% decrease in false alarms.
This paper outlines the design of a functional open source repository for the R programming language, highlighting key considerations and lessons learned from this endeavor.

In a study examining the relationship between a treatment and an outcome, it's often the case that covariates are incomplete, which can lead to biased estimates when ignored. To address this issue, researchers have employed methods like instrumental variable analysis and propensity score matching to account for unobserved variables. However, when multiple missing variables exist, these approaches are often combined but their limitations are still unclear. To address this knowledge gap, this study proposes a new method that utilizes doubly robust estimation to account for both observed and unobserved variables. Theoretical results show that this approach provides unbiased estimates when either the outcome model or the treatment model is correctly specified, and also achieves consistent estimates when both are correctly specified. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that this approach can be easily implemented in high-dimensional settings and provides empirical evidence to support its effectiveness.

The limit of the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, when evaluated at specific points, is found to be equal to a specific value, which can be expressed using a combination of the natural logarithm and the inverse hyperbolic tangent. This result can be used to develop asymptotic expansions for the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, under certain conditions.

The DIPL framework, a novel approach to inductive procedure learning, has been shown to replicate human learning patterns in complex tasks. This study further validates DIPL's effectiveness by applying it to a real-world scenario - the creation of a robotic system capable of pouring liquid from one container to another. The results demonstrate that DIPL's learning process closely mirrors human problem-solving strategies, and the system successfully develops a range of adaptable procedures to tackle the pouring challenge.

The rapid expansion of fake news and machine-generated deceit is causing significant harm to society, necessitating advanced detection methods. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a pre-trained language model, specifically fine-tuning it for text generation, and subsequently leveraging its capabilities for text classification. Our proposed method is validated through experimentation with three prominent language models, resulting in notable improvements over existing benchmarks. Furthermore, we examine the effects of training data size on model performance and provide recommendations for potential future research directions.

We establish that the composite of all $D_4$ extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$ forms a splitting field for torsion-structure rich elliptic curves. This is achieved through the development of a novel approach to class field theory, which we term 'admissible theory', and its application to $D_4$ extensions. Furthermore, we provide a detailed description of the admissible theory of $D_4$ extensions over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-1},\sqrt{2})$.

We investigate a non-uniform qubit array, where a qubit is continuously driven on resonance, leading to dephasing in adjacent qubits due to wavefunction mixing. Our analysis shows that this dephasing can be represented as a localized, non-uniform exchange interaction. By applying the Magnus expansion, we derive an effective, time-periodic Hamiltonian that describes the qubit array's behavior. This effective Hamiltonian enables us to identify a unique, non-uniform ground state and calculate its associated energy. Our results demonstrate that this ground state exhibits a non-trivial, non-uniform phase, characterized by a non-zero Berry phase. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phase is directly related to the qubit array's non-uniform exchange interaction. Our findings suggest that this approach can be used to engineer non-trivial, non-uniform phases in quantum systems.

A focused crawler is designed to efficiently discover and retrieve web pages relevant to a specific subject, such as news or products, while minimizing the number of pages to be crawled. This study presents a novel, multi-strategy approach to subject-focused crawling that integrates three distinct techniques: a rule-based method, a machine learning algorithm, and a content similarity model. The proposed system is tested on a real-world platform using real-time queries and demonstrates the effectiveness of its different components.

Process data is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of information systems. A new method called Process Mining utilizes event records to identify and rectify process inefficiencies. This study examines the integration of Process Java, a process mining technique, with JavaServer Faces, a web-based platform, to enhance process analysis capabilities within these systems. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of automatically extracting process data from JavaServer Faces web logs and utilizing Process Java to analyze and optimize the associated business processes.

Seismic data analysis relies heavily on low-rank factorizations, but these methods become less effective as frequency increases. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a new approach that combines the benefits of low-rank techniques with the high-frequency capabilities of the Fourier domain. Our method, the "seismic 'filter'" (SSF), enables efficient processing of seismic data at various frequencies, including higher frequencies, by leveraging low-rank approximations. This approach is demonstrated through numerical examples, including the application of the SSF to the 2020 CFP wide-azimuth survey, which shows improved results in high-frequency data analysis.

Metalenses with quadratic phase profiles are known to minimize chromatic and off-axis aberrations, but their performance is often compromised by high pixel counts and low numerical aperture. This study demonstrates that these issues can be resolved by designing metalenses with non-paraxial phase profiles, which can achieve high pixel counts and high numerical apertures simultaneously. The research focuses on metalenses with a single phase-pixel design, which can achieve high pixel counts and high numerical apertures. The findings show that non-paraxial phase metalenses can achieve a numerical aperture of 1.55 with just 5 phase-pixels and 1.80 with 7 phase-pixels, which is a significant improvement over previous designs. The research also explores the practicality of these metalenses by comparing their performance with that of traditional paraxial phase metalenses.
